title: Explainable Token-level Noise Filtering for LLM Fine-tuning
one_liner: When you fine-tune an LLM, most training tokens are noise; XTF scores each token on three attributes and masks gradients from the weak ones.
lead: Fine-tuning teaches a large language model a new task by training on examples. The problem: examples are written sentence-by-sentence, but the model learns token-by-token. This mismatch means many individual tokens in each example actually hurt learning. XTF gives every token a report card—three scores that say how useful it is—and then silently drops the bad tokens from training, improving final accuracy by up to 13.7%.

problem.h2: Training examples are built at the sentence level, but models learn at the token level
paras: When you fine-tune an LLM, you give it sentences like 'The capital of France is Paris.' The model trains on every single token: The, capital, of, France, is, Paris. But not every token carries useful information for learning the task. Some tokens are just filler because the model already predicted them correctly during pretraining (no new knowledge), or they do not belong to the task's domain (off-topic), or they contradict what the task is trying to teach.

A naive approach: use all tokens as-is. This seems obvious, but it has a hidden cost. Tokens that mislead the model (a word that appears in the input but should not appear in the output) create wrong learning signals. Tokens the model already knew before fine-tuning are redundant. Tokens unrelated to the task just add noise. The model has to learn despite the noise, which makes training slower and less accurate.

callout.html: Score every token on how useful it is, keep only the useful ones, and mask out the rest during training.

steps.text: Run the full example through the base model and see which tokens it focuses on internally (attention scores measure where the model looks when reading). High attention means the model thinks that token matters for understanding.
Check if the base model already predicts each token correctly; if yes, it is redundant and teaches nothing.
Compare each token's learned representation (a list of numbers learned during pretraining) to the average of all task tokens; distant ones are off-topic.
Tokens scoring low on one or more attributes are marked as noise.
During fine-tuning, silence the learning signals (gradients are the direction the weights should move) from noisy tokens so they do not change the model.

paras: XTF changes which tokens contribute to learning. The training dataset stays the same, but the model now learns only from high-scoring tokens and ignores low-scoring ones.

hidden.name: token contribution score
paras: Most datasets do not tell you which tokens are actually useful for learning. The paper introduces a way to measure it: for each token, assign a score on three dimensions—reasoning importance (does the model focus on this token when reading the input?), knowledge newness (does the model already predict this token?), and task relevance (does this token belong to the task domain?)—and combine them into a usefulness judgment.

XTF estimates each score using the base model itself: by watching where the model's internal attention mechanism looks (which tokens it focuses on), you learn reasoning importance; by checking if the model's current prediction is correct, you learn newness (if it already gets it right, the token is redundant); and by comparing each token's learned number-list to the average of all task tokens, you learn relevance.

heat.caption: Darker means higher score on that attribute. France is hot on all three. The is cold on most.

reads.html: A token is useful if the model's internal attention focuses on it (reasoning importance), if the model does not already predict it correctly (knowledge newness), and if it matches the task's domain vocabulary (task relevance).

Reasoning importance uses the model's attention values. Knowledge newness uses the probability that the model already predicts the token correctly. Task relevance uses distance between the token's learned representation and the average task representation.

mechanism.h2: Why filtering noisy tokens improves fine-tuning
paras: During fine-tuning, the model learns by comparing its predictions to the desired output, calculating how wrong it was (the loss), and nudging its weights in the direction that reduces that loss. Each token contributes a learning signal. Some tokens are useful: they point the model toward the right answer (the model should focus on them, or they teach something new). Other tokens are noise: the model already knows them, or they are off-topic, or they conflict with the task. These create wrong learning signals, pulling the model in the wrong direction.

When you mask the gradients from noisy tokens, you remove the misleading signals before they move the weights. The model's updates are then driven only by tokens that genuinely teach it something new and task-relevant. This removes the contradiction and makes training cleaner: the model does not waste effort learning to satisfy tokens that should not matter for the task.

stages.s: Score each token on three axes

math.words: gradient after filtering equals original gradient multiplied by a mask; mask is 1 for kept tokens and 0 for filtered tokens
math.equation: g_filtered = M * g_original, where M_i = 1 if token_i passes filters, 0 otherwise
symbols: the gradient update that actually moves the weights
the gradient computed from all tokens before filtering
the mask: 1 to keep token i, 0 to silence it
the i-th token in the training example

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Token 1 (France): RI=4, KN=3, TR=4 -> all high -> M_1 = 1. Gradient for this token counts fully.
Token 2 (of): RI=1, KN=2, TR=2 -> all low -> M_2 = 0. Gradient for this token is zeroed out.
Token 3 (The): RI=1, KN=3, TR=1 -> mixed, but relevance fails -> M_3 = 0. Gradient zeroed.
Result: only useful tokens drive weight updates. Noisy signals are removed before they mislead training.

math.note: By zeroing the gradient from noisy tokens, the weight update comes only from good signals. This works because the noisy signals are contradictory and pull in wrong directions; removing them means the weight change is guided only by useful tokens.

charts.title: Standard fine-tuning (all tokens)
charts.note: Model learns, but also absorbs noise from irrelevant tokens.

charts.title: XTF filtered fine-tuning
charts.note: By silencing noisy tokens before they move the weights, the model learns faster from the clean signal. Useful tokens all push the weights in the same direction (toward learning the task); noisy tokens push against them. Remove the noisy pushes, and the useful signals steer the weights more directly toward the answer. Real results show up to 13.7% improvement.

items.html: If you filter out too many tokens, you remove useful signal along with the noise. The model learns from too few examples and underfits.
Attention scores, prediction accuracy, and semantic distance are proxies. They sometimes miss subtle usefulness or mis-flag a token as noise.
Task relevance is computed by comparing to the task domain average. If the task is very different from pretraining, this score is unreliable.
Tune the threshold on a validation set. Test different scoring methods. Use XTF as a pre-processing step to augment data, not replace it entirely.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny fine-tuning job: take a base model, a small training set (20 examples, 30 tokens each), and a test set. Run standard fine-tuning on all tokens. Run XTF filtering (score each token, remove the bottom 40%). Fine-tune again. Measure accuracy on the test set for both runs. Plot accuracy over training steps. The filtered version should reach higher accuracy with the same number of training steps, or reach the same accuracy in fewer steps, because the weight updates are no longer pulled in contradictory directions by noisy tokens.
demo.metric_eq: speed_gain = steps_unfiltered / steps_filtered to reach target_accuracy
demo.closing: The core claim is that filtering noise-only tokens removes the contradictory signals that pull weights in the wrong direction. Measure that the filtered version reaches the target accuracy in fewer training steps than the unfiltered version. This proves that the noisy tokens were slowing learning (not helping it), not that you are losing information.
